title: Parliament Clears Tougher Anti-Paper Leak Law After NEET Crisis
excerpt: Both houses of Parliament have passed the Public Examinations Amendment Bill 2026, introducing up to 10 years' imprisonment and ₹50 lakh fines for exam fraud, as PM Modi vows to dismantle the 'paper mafia.'
body:
• Parliament passed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, with the Rajya Sabha clearing it on July 30 after Lok Sabha approval on July 29.
  • Penalties for paper leaks jump to 5–10 years’ imprisonment and fines up to ₹50 lakh; organised exam fraud carries up to ₹10 crore in fines.
  • The bill mandates two-month investigation deadlines and fast-track courts to complete trials within three months of chargesheet filing.
  • PM Modi announced a task force led by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani to overhaul India’s examination system using technology.

India’s Parliament has cleared the toughest anti-paper leak legislation in the country’s history, capping a turbulent monsoon session dominated by the NEET exam scandal and weeks of youth protests that forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The Rajya Sabha passed the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 on Thursday, July 30, a day after the Lok Sabha approved it by voice vote. The bill now awaits President Droupadi Murmu’s assent to become law.

What the Law Changes

The amendment significantly stiffens penalties under the original 2024 anti-paper leak act, which was itself enacted after earlier NEET irregularities. Individuals found guilty of leaking question papers or using unfair means now face a minimum of five years’ imprisonment, extendable to 10 years, along with fines of up to ₹50 lakh — up from the previous ceiling of three to five years and ₹10 lakh.

Service providers complicit in exam fraud face fines of up to ₹5 crore and an eight-year ban on conducting examinations, double the earlier four-year prohibition. Directors and senior management who connive in offences face five to 10 years’ imprisonment.

For organised examination rackets — the “paper mafia” networks that have compromised exams conducted by agencies including the UPSC, SSC, railway recruitment boards, and the National Testing Agency (NTA) — the bill prescribes seven to 10 years’ imprisonment and fines of up to ₹10 crore.

“Any group organising paper leak, those who play with the future of the country’s children, will not go unpunished.”

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

Fast-Track Courts and Investigation Deadlines

Beyond harsher penalties, the bill introduces strict procedural timelines. Investigations must be completed within two months, and special courts will conduct daily hearings with a target of completing trials within three months after the chargesheet is filed. State governments and Union Territory administrations can designate fast-track courts for cases under the law, and the Centre retains the power to create special task forces for investigations.

Union Minister of State Jitendra Singh, who introduced the bill on July 27, told Parliament that 52 FIRs had been registered since the original anti-paper leak law took effect in 2024. New Education Minister Prahlad Joshi, who replaced Pradhan, said the amendment would “dismantle the paper leak ecosystem and increase transparency, credibility and fairness in the examination process.”

The Crisis Behind the Bill

The legislation follows the cancellation of the NEET undergraduate medical entrance exam after question papers were leaked in May, forcing roughly two million candidates to retake the test. More than a dozen student suicides were linked to the cancellation, according to Reuters.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, founded by activist Abhijeet Dipke, led a 36-day protest campaign that drew tens of thousands to Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. Activist Sonam Wangchuk joined with a hunger strike on June 28, and his forced hospitalisation on July 18 galvanised larger crowds. Clashes on July 20, when police used tear gas and baton charges on marchers near Parliament, marked the most intense confrontation.

The protests ended on July 22 after the government agreed to Pradhan’s resignation, exam system reforms, dropping cases against protesters, and compensating families of students who died by suicide.

Nilekani Task Force and Broader Reforms

On July 26, Modi announced a task force headed by tech entrepreneur Nandan Nilekani — co-founder of Infosys and architect of India’s Aadhaar digital identity system — to overhaul the country’s examination infrastructure with greater use of technology.

“Our examination system should be trustworthy, should be transparent, and the system should make maximum use of technology.”

— Narendra Modi, via social media

Political Fireworks in Parliament

The bill’s passage was far from smooth. Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi accused the government of mishandling the NEET crisis and alleged that Home Minister Amit Shah had ordered police action against student protesters — a claim Union Minister Jitendra Singh rejected. Gandhi also alleged RSS influence over educational institutions and curricula.

In the Rajya Sabha, Leader of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge dismissed the amendments as largely cosmetic, saying changes were “limited to figures” and “would not make any difference.” Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi’s remarks about new Education Minister Joshi during the Lok Sabha debate were expunged from House records.

What Comes Next

The bill awaits presidential assent. Once enacted, the Nilekani task force’s recommendations on technology-driven exam reforms will shape the next phase of changes. For the millions of Indian students preparing for competitive exams — including many with aspirations to study or work abroad — the law signals the government’s intent to restore credibility to a system that underpins career pathways across the country.
nri_angle: For millions of Indian students preparing for competitive exams that shape career pathways domestically and abroad, the tougher law and Nilekani-led technology reforms aim to restore trust in an examination system central to their aspirations.
